newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan urges Beijing to acknowledge China divided.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan urges Beijing to acknowledge China divided.

text.p: Taiwan President Lee Teng-hui on Monday urged communist Beijing to accept that China is divided and acknowledge his island's sovereignty, saying only this would lead to better ties and the goal of national unification.

Lee, addressing the constitutional assembly, urged Taiwan's business community to put the survival of the Nationalist-ruled island's democracy ahead of profits and "refrain from temptation" in China's economic boom.
Taiwan screens mainland-bound investment and bans financing of major Chinese infrastructure projects, aiming to avoid overdependence on its rival's economy.

Lee urged Beijing to stop characterising his government's every move as promoting Taiwan's independence, as this was not only unproductive but also a moot point since the sovereignty of its exiled Republic of China had been a fact for 86 years.
"This kind of prejudice neither helps exchanges across the Taiwan strait nor benefits people's welfare," Lee said.
Lee said Beijing's People's Republic of China must accept the continued existence of the Republic of China on Taiwan despite its 1949 civil war defeat on the mainland.
By accepting that the rival states were equal political entities, Beijing could best ensure progress towards their common goal of a unified China, Lee told the National Assembly.
"We will never waver in our insistence on a single China that is unified as a new China through democracy, freedom and the equitable distribution of wealth," Lee said.
"Whether relations across the Taiwan strait can have genuine interaction depends on whether the Chinese communist authorities can practically face the reality of one China divided."
Beijing, whose communist army toppled Chiang Kai-shek's Nationalist republic in 1949, calls Lee's government an illegitimate power that must accept communist sovereignty.
Beijing opposes creation of a breakaway Republic of Taiwan, vowing to use force to thwart an ideal that Taiwan opinion polls show has strong, though not universal, support.
China has hinted that it saw Friday's National Assembly vote to marginalise a largely redundant Taiwan provincial government as more evidence of what it brands "splittist" intent.
Mainland Foreign Ministry spokesman Tang Guoqiang reiterated Beijing's bottom line on Taiwan's current and future status.
"No matter what changes occur in Taiwan, one fact cannot be changed: Taiwan is a part of China," Tang said on Thursday.
Taipei has long maintained a Taiwan provincial authority separate from the national state to support its increasingly untenable claim to be the sole legitimate sovereign of all China.
With Beijing refusing to acknowledge the exiled republic, Taipei bans official links with Beijing -- though both have tolerated an explosion of economic and other unofficial ties.

Lee said Taipei would not give up its defiance of Beijing's diplomatic embargo to expand its international "living space", a drive that includes annual attempts, easily thwarted by Beijing, to secure a United Nations seat for Taiwan's 21 million people.

Lee said that as long as Beijing squeezed Taiwan, it had no choice but to limit interaction with the mainland, where despite tough restrictions Taiwan interests have managed to invest more than US$30 billion since a late 1980s political thaw.

"Before the hostile status across the strait vanishes, I hope our local business community can realise that national survival and development are far more important than business opportunities," Lee said.
"Only by supporting the government's policy can we ensure an advantageous position in peaceful cross-strait competition."
Lee said Taipei and Beijing could overcome their differences with time.

"After nearly 50 years of separate rule...we need enough time to increase understanding and reduce distance. We are willing to continue our effort to strive for Chinese's common welfare with our utmost patience and action," he said.
